title: Toward Regenerative Sustainability: A Passive Design Comfort Assessment Method of Indoor Environment
central_proposition: This paper proposes a passive design comfort assessment model for the indoor environment, encompassing physiological, biophilic, and psychological/social aspects of comfort, aimed at enhancing building users’ health and well-being, thus contributing to regenerative sustainability goals.

concept_definitions.name: Regenerative Sustainability
concept_definitions.definition: harmonized co-evolving of all living beings, e.g., humans with nature, aimed at creatively enhancing vitality, viability, biodiversity and complexity.

concept_definitions.name: Salutogenesis
concept_definitions.definition: health-inducing factors, encompassing not only physical and biochemical parameters (essential for the survival), but also cultural, subcultural and individual responses to a constantly changing environment, crucial for achieving sociological and psychological homeostasis.

concept_definitions.name: Bioclimatic Architecture
concept_definitions.definition: ecologically adequate, energy rational integration of the built environment within the natural environmental flow, aimed at achieving comfort in an overall sense.

concept_definitions.name: Biophilia
concept_definitions.definition: inducing positive environmental impacts and the enhancement of people's physical and mental health, productivity and well-being.

concept_definitions.name: Comfort
concept_definitions.definition: a sensitized and satisfying relation between the human body and its immediate surroundings.

argument_structure: The paper builds its argument by first reviewing existing sustainability paradigms, identifying gaps in current assessment systems regarding holistic comfort, passive design, and biophilic/psychological aspects. It then proposes a new Passive Design Comfort Assessment Model, detailing its six categories (thermal, air quality, visual, acoustic, biophilic, psychological/social) with specific criteria, indicators, and passive design measures. The relevance of this model is supported by a comprehensive literature review and validated by expert consultation and comparative analysis with existing sustainability rating systems.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The proposed causal mechanism is that by integrating comprehensive passive design measures and holistic comfort aspects (physiological, biophilic, psychological/social) into architectural design, the built environment can foster an innate human connection to nature, support adaptive human capacities, and provide salutogenic conditions. This leads to improved physical, mental, and social health and well-being for building users, thereby achieving regenerative sustainability goals.

findings.consequent: Enhanced vitality, viability, biodiversity, and complexity of all living beings (humans with nature)
findings.mechanism: By fostering harmonized co-evolution and life-supporting relationships between the built and natural environment.
findings.quote: The regenerative developmental approach refers to the harmonized co-evolving of all living beings, e.g., humans with nature, aimed at creatively enhancing vitality, viability, biodiversity and complexity.

findings.consequent: Improved health and well-being of building users
findings.mechanism: By focusing on health-inducing factors and fostering physical, mental, and social well-being, rather than merely preventing disease.
findings.quote: in the architectural realm, the salutogenic approach relates to a comprehensive, holistic research of design and building-related factors for improving the health and well-being of building users.

findings.consequent: Healthier and more energy-efficient indoor environment
findings.mechanism: By leveraging natural adaptive abilities to thermal changes, reducing reliance on mechanical ventilation, and providing optimal thermal comfort conditions.
findings.quote: applying passive design measures of solar architecture underlines our natural ability to adapt to thermal changes in the environment (air temperature), leading to the diminished usage of mechanical ventilation, which finally results in a healthier and more energy-efficient indoor environment.

findings.mechanism: By filtering dust particles and decreasing concentrations of CO, CO2, tobacco smoke, and other harmful air particles.
findings.quote: Natural ventilation and vegetation filtrate dust particles, decrease the concentration of CO, CO2, tobacco smoke and other harmful air particles.

findings.consequent: Optimal indoor humidity levels and improved air quality
findings.mechanism: By absorbing water during high humidity and releasing it during low humidity, naturally regulating indoor moisture.
findings.quote: Hygroscopicity is a property of porous earth-originated materials... which... enable the maintenance of optimal humidity levels, hence naturally improving air quality within indoor environment.

findings.consequent: Modulated visual perception and indoor atmosphere
findings.mechanism: By influencing psychological effects, such as relaxation (warm colors, lower illuminance) or stimulation (cold colors, higher illuminance), and affecting emotional and physical well-being.
findings.quote: Color, as a property of light, affects the visual perception and atmosphere indoors, thus the visual comfort.

findings.consequent: Masked unwanted noise and improved acoustic comfort
findings.mechanism: By producing pleasant natural sounds that are closer to human ear, thereby prevailing over background noise.
findings.quote: moving water features (fountains, waterfalls) may significantly mask noise (the pleasant sound of water is closer to human ear, thus prevailing/'masking' the background noise).

findings.mechanism: By providing pleasant sensations (fresh air, breeze, aromatic plants, bird song) that contribute to physical and psychological well-being and stress reduction.
findings.quote: Gardens enable pleasant sensations and perceptions of nature: from inhaling fresh air rich in oxygen, feeling breeze on the skin, watching and smelling aromatic plants, to listening bird song, which all contributes to health and healing.

findings.consequent: Positive effect on human senses and health/well-being
findings.mechanism: By their appearance (patina, age), agreeable scent, and pleasant texture, connecting users to the environment and fostering a sense of 'rootness' and identity.
findings.quote: Natural materials have positive effect on our senses by the appearance with patina, carrying a message about material age, agreeable scent (e.g., wood), and pleasant, 'inviting' to touch texture. They connect us with the environment they derived from and support 'rootness' in life...

findings.antecedent: Connection to natural cycles (light, activity, sound, scents, evolving/decay)
findings.mechanism: By providing diverse sensory perception and awareness of natural phenomena, stimulating senses and fostering a dynamic relationship with the environment.
findings.quote: Life energies affecting our health involve aspects of connection to natural cycles: seasonal and daily rhythms of light, activity, sound and scents, evolving and decay.

findings.mechanism: By leading to inactivity of senses, decreased levels of focus, attention, sensitivity, and perception.
findings.quote: A deprivation of change leads to the inactivity of senses, decreased levels of focus, attention, sensitivity, perception, which finally results in lethargy and negative moods.

findings.antecedent: Moderate, constant, controlled change in perceptive comfort aspects
findings.mechanism: By supporting thermal and visual variability, functional adaptability, and preventing overstimulation.
findings.quote: moderate, constant, controlled change within all perceptive comfort aspects is favorable.

findings.mechanism: By enabling connection to the outside world, providing information about time, weather, and surroundings, and reducing stress.
findings.quote: A view is a basic visual, psychological need, implying daylight and windows. View enables connection to the outside world and nature, provides information about the time of the day, weather conditions, surrounding, thus helping us orienting in space and time.

findings.consequent: Enhanced feeling of identity and 'genius loci'
findings.mechanism: By carrying the trace of time and being transformed by natural factors, creating a sense of belonging to the place of origins.
findings.quote: Autochthone materials derived from the surrounding carry the trace of time, creating a feeling of building belonging to the place of origins, with regard to being transformed by the natural influential factors.

findings.antecedent: Spatial adaptability and flexibility (layout, size, use)
findings.consequent: Enhanced psychological/social comfort and social support
findings.mechanism: By allowing adjustment to occupants' needs and usage modes, fostering equality (e.g., round tables), and increasing social interaction.
findings.quote: Spatial adaptability and flexibility, in terms of simply adjusting to changes of the occupants' needs and usage mode, represents a significant factor of psychological/social aspects of comfort.

findings.mechanism: By avoiding intimidating effects of too high and immense spaces, fostering a sense of comfort and belonging.
findings.quote: Too high and immense a space can have an intimidating effect on users, while human scale rooms inspire pleasant and welcoming atmosphere.

findings.antecedent: Soft and rounded shapes in interior space
findings.mechanism: By inducing specific psychological reactions that contrast with the intellectual clarity and ascetic calmness associated with hard, angled, and rectangular forms.
findings.quote: shapes can induce psychological reactions, e.g., hard, angled and rectangular forms stimulate intellectual clarity followed by feelings of ascetic calmness to repulsive inaccessibility, while soft and rounded strives at sensuality varying from welcoming to oppressively enwrapping.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Implementing passive design measures (e.g., solar architecture, natural ventilation, hygroscopic materials) will lead to a healthier and more energy-efficient indoor environment by reducing reliance on mechanical ventilation and regulating indoor air quality and humidity.

Integrating biophilic elements (e.g., plants, water features, natural materials, nature views) into indoor environments will increase building users' physical, mental, and emotional well-being, and reduce stress levels.

Designing indoor spaces with consideration for psychological/social comfort aspects (e.g., constant/controlled change, adaptable layouts, human scale, specific color schemes, tactile natural materials) will enhance users' cognitive functions, mood, sense of identity, and social interaction.
bridge_warrants: The proposed model integrates salutogenesis by focusing on health-inducing factors in architectural design.
The model incorporates biophilic design principles by emphasizing the integration of natural elements and forms to enhance human-nature connection.
The model aligns with bioclimatic architecture by prioritizing passive design measures for energy efficiency and comfort.
The model addresses the need for holistic sustainability by combining physiological, biophilic, and psychological/social comfort aspects.
methodological_critiques: Current sustainability rating systems (LEED, BREEAM, CASBEE, LBC, WELL) insufficiently incorporate relevant regenerative design topics, especially comprehensive comfort aspects, passive design measures, and qualitative biophilic/psychological/social factors.
Existing systems are dominantly focused on energy efficiency and minimized negative environmental impact, neglecting the regenerative potential for positive human and environmental outcomes.
model_structure: The paper proposes a 'Passive Design Comfort Assessment Model' for the indoor environment, structured around six comfort-related categories: Thermal Comfort, Air Quality, Visual Comfort, Acoustic Comfort, Biophilic Aspects of Comfort, and Psychological/Social Aspects of Comfort. Each category is further broken down into specific criteria, indicators, and passive design measures. The model aims to provide a holistic framework for assessing and enhancing health and well-being in buildings.
limitations: The proposed research has a generic character, as comfort assessment categories, indicators, and passive measures are considered regardless of specific architectural typologies.
Diverse requirements depending on building types may necessitate the introduction of new and more typology-specific comfort-related categories, indicators, and measures.

paper_metadata.title: Toward Regenerative Sustainability: A Passive Design Comfort Assessment Method of Indoor Environment
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Toward Regenerative Sustainability: A Passive Design Comfort Assessment Method of Indoor Environment
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The fact that people spend a major part of their lifetime indoors, together with the lethal COVID-19 pandemic which caused people to spend even more time inside buildings, has drawn attention to the significance of achieving Agenda 2030 SD goal number three: good health and well-being, in reference to the indoor environment. The research subject is the health and well-being of building users explored through the sustainable (passive) design principles having an impact on the comfort and quality of the indoor environment. It is set within a regenerative sustainability framework encompassing the physiological, biophilic, psychological and social aspects of comfort. The Comfort Assessment Model’s categories, to some extent, rely on the first author’s doctoral thesis, with further modifications regarding the passive design criteria and indicators. A comparative analysis of the model with international sustainability certification (rating) systems has been performed, proving the significance of introducing more passive design comfort (health) related criteria into sustainability assessment models. In addition, a focus group of expert architects contributed to the research conclusions by responding to a questionnaire addressing the issues of sustainability, comfort and passive design, in terms of the health and well-being of building users, which confirmed the relevance of applied passive design measures for providing comfort indoors and fulfilling sustainable development goals.
